Performance evaluation and microbial community analysis of microaerobic 
pretreatment on thermophilic dry anaerobic digestion 
Feng Zhen a,b,c,d, Xinjian Luo b,c,d, Tao Xing b,c,d, Yongming Sun b,c,d, Xiaoying Kong b,c,d,**, 
Wenzhe Li a,e,* 
a College of Engineering, Northeast Agriculture University, Harbin, 150030, China 
b Guangzhou Institute of Energy Conversion, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Guangzhou, 510640, China 
c CAS Key Laboratory of Renewable Energy, Guangzhou, 510640, China 
d Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of New and Renewable Energy Research and Development, Guangzhou, 510640, China 
e Key Laboratory of Agricultural Renewable Resources Utilization Technology and Equipment in Cold Areas of Heilongjiang Province, Harbin, 150030, China   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Microaerobic pretreatment 
Dry anaerobic digestion 
Microbial community 
Corn stalk 
Methane production 
A B S T R A C T   
In this study, microaerobic pretreatment (MP) was used to improve the system stability and biogas production 
performance of the thermophilic dry anaerobic digestion (AD). The results showed that proper MP made the AD 
have better methane-producing performance and the maximum cumulative methane production was 108.31 mL/ 
g VS with an oxygen load of 5 mL/g VS, which was 13.20 % higher than that of control group (G1, 95.68 mL/g 
VS). Specific microaerobic conditions promoted the generation of volatile fatty acid (VFA) and reduced propionic 
acid content in the digestive system. In addition, the volatile solid (VS) removal rate of the digestive substrates 
was improved in the presence of limited oxygen, which can reduce environmental risks. Microbial community 
diversity indicated that MP increased the relative abundance of Firmicutes to promote substrate hydrolysis and 
accelerated the growth of hydrogenotrophic methanogens to improve AD performance.   
1. Introduction 
As an environmentally friendly and efficient method, AD technology 
has been widely used in the disposal of organic waste such as food waste, 
sludge, crop stalk and animal manure, which can convert organic matter 
into methane energy via microorganisms [1–3]. At present, three major 
AD technologies have been studied: wet (TS ≤10 %), hemi-dry (10 % 
<TS < 15 %) and dry (TS ≥15 %) AD, also called high-solid AD [4]. 
Generally, hemi-dry or dry AD is more attractive with less water, smaller 
digester and higher volume biogas production. Whereas, it is less effi­
cient than wet AD for mass transfer, heat transfer, and stirring in 
anaerobic digester [5]. Therefore, low microbial access to substrates and 
potential accumulation of toxicity and inhibitors (e.g. volatile fatty acids 
and ammonia) may occur in dry AD, which is detrimental to the 
digestive system [6]. 
Previous studies have demonstrated that the hydrolysis of the 
digestive substrate could be enhanced by the introduction of limited 
oxygen [7]. Tsapekos, et al. [8] showed that the maximum production of 
biogas was obtained by injecting 5 mL O2/g VS for 3 days, which was 7.2 
% higher than that of the untreated wheat straw. Lim, et al. [9] also 
reported that there was an increase in the hydrolysis rate of AD due to 
greater diversity of bacteria and higher abundance of Firmicutes in 
microaerobic conditions. The potential mechanism of enhanced AD may 
be that the addition of microoxygen inhibit the formation of toxic me­
tabolites (such as lactic acid and ethanol) and promote the synthesis of 
substances required for the stability of anaerobic cell membranes [10]. 
The rapid growth of facultative bacteria can produce more cellulolytic 
and proteolytic enzymes [11]. Therefore, as an environmental protec­
tion and economic pretreatment process, MP is more feasible to improve 
the performance of dry AD. 
In addition, thermophilic conditions are often used in dry AD to 
obtain higher destruction rates of organic solids and superior growth of 
microorganisms [12]. Compared to mesophilic digestion, higher biogas 
production can be obtained in a shorter residence time by thermophilic 
digestion, which realizes a greater organic load rate. Fern´andez-Ro­
dríguez, et al. [13] observed that the methane production of the organic 
fraction of municipal solid waste (OFMSW) at 55 ℃ was 27 % higher 
than that at 35 ℃, and the operation time to obtain the same methane

production was reduced from 40 to 20 days. Suhartini, et al. [14] 
showed that the biogas and methane productivity for thermophilic 
digestion of sugar beet pulp was higher than that of mesophilic diges­
tion, and could operate at higher organic loading rates, while the latter 
showed signs of instability. In addition, an attention has been found that 
aerobic or anaerobic thermophilic bacteria have higher hydrolysis ca­
pabilities, which can be seen as a potential way to accelerate the hy­
drolytic process [15]. 
Based on the above analysis, different oxygen loads were passed into 
the digester for a thermophilic dry anaerobic digestion and attempted to 
improve the system stability and biogas production performance of 
thermophilic dry AD by MP. Therefore, the aims of this study were: (1) 
to analyze the performance of the biogas production at different 
microaerobic conditions; (2) to investigate the variation of VFA content 
and VS remove rate; (3) to explore the effects of MP on microbial 
community and diversity. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Material and inoculum 
Corn Stalk (CS) was collected from Zengcheng, Guangdong Province, 
China, which was crushed by a pulverizer (XB-HP, xiaobao,China) to 
obtain small particles of less than 40 meshes, and then stored in a 
desiccator at room temperature until further processing. The inoculum 
was derived from a thermophilic continuous stirred tank reactor with CS 
as substrates. The characteristics of raw material and inoculum are listed 
in Table 1. 
2.2. Digester setup and operation 
Anaerobic digestion experiments were performed in a 500 mL 
brucellae flask digester. The CS, inoculum and deionized water were 
placed to the digester to form 150 g of effective digestive liquid with a 
TS of 16.76 %. A certain proportion of the air was pumped with a vac­
uum pump and the same volume of pure oxygen was injected by the 
syringe, which created a different micro-oxygen environment. The 
experimental design was shown in Table 2. Finally, all digesters were 
operated at 55 ℃ for 35 days. 
The biogas samples of AD were analyzed every day, and the analysis 
interval increased gradually with time. To analyze the system state of 
AD, samples were taken at the bottom of the digester on the 2nd, 15th 
and 28th days, respectively, which were used to determine the metab­
olites and the community succession of bacteria and archaea. All sam­
ples were stored in a refrigerator at -20 ℃ before determination and 
three parallels were set in each experimental group. 
2.3. Analytical methods 
TS and VS were determined according to the Standard method [16]. 
The carbon and nitrogen contents of the samples were determined by an 
element analyzer (Vario EL Cube, Germany). The pH value was deter­
mined by a pH meter. 
The biogas content of N2, CH4 and CO2 was determined by Shimadzu 
high-efficiency gas chromatograph (GC2014, Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan) 
via a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). The VFAs contents (acetic 
acid, propionic acid and butyric acid) were measured by the HPLC 
system (waters e2695), equipped with a refractive index detector (SH- 
1011). The column temperature was 50 ℃ and the mobile phase was 
0.005 mM H2SO4 with a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min. 
2.4. Analysis procedure of microbial community 
16S rDNA sequencing of sample sequencing was commissioned by 
Sangon Biotech (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. to understand the impact of 
microoxygen on the ecology of digester microbial community. 
2.4.1. Sampling and DNA extraction 
Triplicate samples from G1 to G4 were collected on days 2, 14, and 
28, and marked as G1−2d, G1−14d, G1−28d, G2−2d, G2−14d, and so 
on. The samples were stored at -20 ℃ for subsequent analysis. Then, the 
genomic DNA of the entire community was extracted with a kit (E.Z.N. 
A™ Mag-Bind Soil DNA Kit, OMEGA), and the extracted DNA concen­
tration was estimated by gel electrophoresis. 
2.4.2. PCR amplification and Sequencing for bioinformatics analysis 
The bacterial 16S rDNA sequence fragment was amplified by uni­
versal primers (515 F and 806R, 5`-GTGCCAGCMGCCGCGGTAA-3` and 
5`-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3`), and then the polymerase chain 
reaction (PCR) assays were performed on each sample. Sequencing was 
performed on an Illumina HiSeq 2000 (Illumina, San Diego, USA). The 
data was pre-processed and then separately analyzed by operational 
taxonomic units (OTUs) clustering and biodiversity analysis by the Ri­
bosomal Database Project (RDP) database (http://rdp.cme.msu.edu 
/misc/resources.jsp).

2.6. Statistical analysis 
The basic data were sorted with Excel 2016 software, and the data 
were statistically analyzed by Origin 2017 (Origin Lab Corporation, 
Northampton, MA, USA). 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Biogas production performance during dry AD 
Methane production is considered to be the main indicator for 
evaluating AD performance, and it is also the primary objective of AD to 
achieve higher methane production. The production and composition 
characteristics of biogas are shown in Fig. 1. Fig. 1(a) shows the cu­
mulative biogas production from day AD under different microoxygen 
loads. Biogas production in all experimental groups was mainly 
concentrated 16 days before anaerobic digestion. The final values 
detected of G1-G4 were 199.41, 215.95, 195.54 and 176.65 mL/g VS, 
respectively. Correspondingly, methane content in all groups fell below 
50 % after 16 days of anaerobic digestion (Fig. 1(b)). The difference was 
that the k of G1 is 0.1107, higher than that of all MP groups (Table 3). 
This suggested that MP could lead to a faster conversion of the digestion 
substrate to simple organic compounds due to a lower hydrolysis con­
stant [19]. 
As can be seen from Fig. 1(c), the daily methane production 
decreased to 5 mL/g VS in all the experimental groups on the 20th day of 
AD, which showed that the effect of MP on the main methanogenic 
period of AD was very weak. During the first five days of AD, the daily 
methane production of G2 and G3 was significantly higher than that of 
G1, while that of G4 was opposite. The result was consistent with λ in 
Table 3, whose descending order was G4 (2.93), G1 (2.34), G2 (2.04), 
and G3 (1.98), respectively. This indicated that proper microaerobic 
made the AD have better methane-producing performance in the early 
stage. However, the oxygen load is important for digestive system, and 
excess oxygen may inhibit the activities of methanogens and reduce 
methane production [20]. For the cumulative methane production 
(Fig. 1(d)), the order observed is G2 > G3 > G1 > G4, the maximum 
detection was 108.31 mL/g VS, which was 13.20 % higher than that of 
G1 (95.68 mL/g VS). The results were similar to the study of Botheju, 
et al. [21], who found that methane production decreased as oxygen 
loads increase range 0–10.1 % (as % of feed COD). 
3.2. VFA concentration and composition analysis 
VFA is an important intermediate in the process of digestive sub­
strates conversion to methane, including metabolites such as acetic acid, 
propionic acid and butyric acid [22]. From Fig. 2, it can be seen that the 
highest concentration of VFA was obtained in G3, which was 10.18 g/L 
and 15.87 % higher than G1 (8.79 g/L) on the second day. Whereas, the 
VFA concentration of G4 was 7.86 g/L, 10.58 % lower than G0. This is 
because higher hydrolysis is achieved in microaerobic conditions with 
specific ranges, which will promote VFA generation. Fu, et al. [19] also 
reported that excessive oxygen would consume some readily available 
organic substrates such as VFA. In addition, for the experimental group 
G1-G4, acetic acid content accounted for 67.35–72.87 % of the total 
VFA, indicating that the methane-producing pathway of acetic acid

played a major role in the initial stage of dry AD. On the 14th day, the 
VFA concentrations of G1-G4 were 12.94, 14.42, 14.45 and 12.94 g/L, 
respectively. It can be inferred that the digestive system may have 
produced inhibition due to excessive accumulation of VFA [6], and the 
decrease of daily methane production also supports above possibility. 
Among them, the contents of acetic acid were significantly reduced 
without accumulation. Whereas, the increased butyric acid contents 
exceeded 8000 mg/L, which indicated that the overaccumulation of 
butyric acid was the main reason for the inhibition of dry AD. On the 
28th day, acid accumulation did not occur in all experimental groups 
with a VFA of 0.78–2.02 g/L, indicating that the substrate s was almost 
degraded. In addition, acetic acid and butyric acid as consumables in 
two methane-producing pathways are beneficial for anaerobic diges­
tion, while the accumulation of propionic acid is a factor limiting 
methane production [23]. An interesting phenomenon was that the 
propionic acid content of G2-G4 was lower than that of G1 at day 2,14, 
and 28 of AD, which may be one of the reasons that MP can increase 
methane production. 
3.3. VS removal rate 
The VS removal rate is a critical indicator for evaluating AD per­
formance, which reflects the amount of substrate recovery and envi­
ronmental benefits, and its higher removal rate will result in lower 
environmental risks [24]. As shown in Fig. 3, the VS removal rate of G1 
was 42.08 %, lower than that of the MP groups (G2-G4) by 29.08 %, 
32.75 % and 10.22 %, respectively. It should be noted that the substrates 
and inocula of AD were identical prior to the initial and final VS mea­
surements in this study. Therefore, other factors on the analysis of VS 
removal rate can be ignored. 
3.4. Analysis of microbial diversity and community 
AD is a complex multi-stage biochemical reaction. As the executor of 
the digestion process, the diversity and abundance of microorganisms 
indirectly reflect the running state of digestive system [25]. During 
digestion, microbial diversity and community vary with the change of 
digestion parameters and time [26]. Therefore, the diversity and struc­
ture of bacteria and archaea under different microaerobic conditions on 
days 2,15, and 28 were analyzed in this study. 
As showed in Table 4, the sequence reads for G1-G4 were 
39,535−75,610 for bacteria and 49,700−83,984 for archaea, with a 
total of 1,024−3,025 and 511–742 OTUs identified for bacteria and 
archaea, respectively. In addition, some related diversity indexes are 
also listed in this table. The Chao1 index for OTUs evaluation was 
1,733.54−3,558.08 for bacteria and 1,437.20–3285.37 for archaea. The 
indexes (Shannon and Simpson) for microbial diversity evaluation were 
1.98–4.41 and 0.03−0.27 for bacteria, respectively, and 2.08–3.01 and 
0.13−0.22 for archaea, respectively. All coverage values greater than 
0.99 indicated that most of the microbial community in the reactors had 
been detected. 
3.4.1. Effects of microaerobic pretreatment on bacterial community 
The community of bacteria at phylum level are shown in Fig. 4(a). 
The phyla with relative abundances greater than 1% in at least one 
sample of all the experimental groups were Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, 
Synergistetes and Proteobacteria. Firmicutes dominated the entire AD 
process for all experimental groups, which produces extracellular en­
zymes (i.e. cellulase, lipase and protease) that promotes the degradation 
of cellulose, fat and proteins [27]. Bacteroidetes play an important role in 
the degradation and VFA generation of organic compounds such as 
carbohydrates and proteins [28]. Some acetogens in Synergistic are 
involved in the conversion of VFA to acetate during AD process, and 
hydrogen can be generated to feed the hydrogenotrophic methanogens 
[29]. Proteobacteria are also capable of hydrolysis and acidogenesis in 
AD [24]. 
On the second day, there was no significant difference in phylum 
level for all the experimental groups due to the initial AD, and Firmicutes, 
as the main phylum, had a relative abundance of 96.35 %, 92.18 %,

96.49 % and 92.42 %, respectively. Subsequently, for all the experi­
mental groups, the relative abundance of Firmicutes decreased, while 
that of Bacteroidetes increased significantly on the 15th day. It can be 
inferred that more acidogenic bacteria are involved in the metabolic 
activities of AD than the second day. In addition, the relative abundance 
of Firmicutes in G2-G4 exceeded that of G0 (73.32 %) by 9.02%–11.65%. 
This was because more oxygen was provided to support the growth and 
metabolism of facultative bacteria under microaerobic conditions [30]. 
It also promoted the production of more hydrolases, which meant that 
the MP has a higher hydrolysis rate. On the 15th day, the relative 
abundance of Firmicutes increased again while that of Bacteroidetes 
decreased, indicating that the acidogens activity was weakened in AD 
process, which was consistent with the changing trend of VFA 
concentration. 
The relative abundance changes of bacterial communities at generic 
level in each experimental group are shown in Fig. 4(b). ten genera with 
a relative abundance greater than 1% were detected, dominated by 
Sinibacillus, Tepidimicrobium and Clostridium. Sinibacillus is a typical 
thermotropic facultative anaerobic bacteria, which is the dominant 
bacteria that degrades organic matter in thermotropic AD [31]. For the 
all experimental groups, the relative abundance of Sinibacillus gradually 
decreased on days 2, 15, and 28. It is not difficult to understand that the 
substrate hydrolysis process is mainly concentrated in the early AD. 
Differently, on the second day of AD, the relative abundance of G1 was 
only 9.8 %, lower than MP groups, whose relative abundance was 9.85 
% (G2), 19.04 % (G3) and 11.68 % (G4), respectively. The results also 
confirmed that the AD with MP had a better hydrolysis rate. The abilities 
of Tepidimicrobium are responsible for degrading cellulose and produc­
ing VFA [32]. Generally, the amount of Tepidimicrobium is considered as 
an indicator for the acidification process [33]. Clostridium is also a genus 
with the strong capacity of hydrolysis and acid production [34]. Both of 
them are responsible for the conversion of molecular organic matter into 
volatile fatty acids. Their relative abundance in G2-G4 was 26.19 %, 
21.91 % and 25.68 %, respectively, higher than that of G1 on the second 
day, while the opposite was the case on the 15th day. The relative 
abundance of G1 was 28.34 %, higher than that of the MP groups from 
10.01–115.35%. The results show that MP has a higher acidogenesis rate 
in the early AD phase.

anaerobic, and oxygen intervention may be disastrous for the activity of 
methanogenic methanogens [35]. Therefore, it is necessary to explore 
the effects of MP on the community of archaea in AD. As can be seen 
from Fig. 5, all classified archaea from the four experimental groups

relative abundance of aceticlastic methanogens in all the experimental 
groups decreased gradually, while that of hydrogenotrophic metha­
nogens increased gradually with the anaerobic digestion time, and the 
change trend of G1 was more obvious. This indicated that the hydro­
genotrophic methanogenic pathway was more advantageous in dry AD, 
and MP further promoted this transformation [38]. Chen, et al. [39] also 
mentioned that MP could remove sulfide and accelerate the growth of 
hydrogenotrophic methanogens to improve AD performance. In addi­
tion, genus Methanobacterium, as a dominant hydrogenotrophic metha­
nogen in this study, has been reported to have limited oxygen tolerance 
[40]. This may be the reason why the relative abundance of Meth­
anobacterium in the MP group was higher than that of G1 on the 15th 
days. 
4. Conclusion 
The present study confirmed that MP could improve the system 
stability and biogas production performance of the thermophilic dry AD. 
The results showed that proper oxygen injection promoted the genera­
tion of VFA during hydrolysis acidogenesis stage and reduced propionic 
acid content throughout the digestive cycle. After digestion, the 
maximum cumulative methane production of 108.31 mL/g VS was ob­
tained at G3, higher than G1 (95.68 mL/g VS) 13.2 %, and higher VS 
removal rate was obtained at the same oxygen load (5 mL/g VS). In 
addition, microbial community diversity indicated that the relative 
abundance of Firmicutes was increased by MP, which facilitated the 
hydrolysis of CS substrate, and the hydrogenotrophic methanogenic 
pathway was strengthened to improve AD performance.
